"Squeeze" means to press something firmly from two or more sides at the same time, usually with your fingers, hands, or body. Think of holding an orange in your palm and pressing it tightly — that is squeezing. The pressure applied from multiple directions is the central image of this word. Every other meaning you'll learn below grows naturally from it.

Pressing to force something out

The most direct use is pressing something to make a substance come out of it. The pressure is the cause; something emerging is the result.

She squeezed the lemon over the salad. He squeezed the toothpaste out of the tube. Squeeze a little glue onto the paper.

This also works more broadly — you can "squeeze the last bit of effort" out of yourself, meaning you extracted absolutely everything you had.

Pressing as a physical gesture of emotion

When you squeeze a person or part of their body, it is usually warm and affectionate — a way of communicating something through touch. It is firm but not painful.

She squeezed his hand to comfort him. He squeezed her in a tight hug. The child squeezed her toy against her chest.

The physical action is identical (pressing firmly), but here the purpose is to express love, support, or reassurance.

Pressing a trigger

In the context of firearms, the correct and precise word is "squeeze" — not "pull."

He squeezed the trigger carefully.

Fitting into a tight physical space

If a space is very narrow but you manage to get through or into it, you squeeze. The idea is that your body is being pressed on both sides as you pass through, like forcing something through a narrow gap.

She squeezed through the small gap in the fence. They squeezed five people into a tiny car. He squeezed past the other passengers. Can you squeeze one more book onto that shelf?

This is extremely common in everyday English. Any time a space is barely enough, "squeeze" is the natural word.

Fitting into a tight schedule

The exact same logic — barely fitting into a tight space — applies to time. When your day is almost full but you manage to fit something in, you squeeze it in.

The doctor can squeeze you in at 4 PM. I squeezed a quick workout into my morning. Can we squeeze this call in before the meeting?

Pressuring someone to extract something from them

When you "squeeze" a person in this sense, you apply pressure on them — through demands, threats, or persistent force — to get money, information, a confession, or something else of value. This use carries a forceful or slightly aggressive tone.

The landlord squeezed the tenants for higher rent. The detective squeezed the suspect for a confession. Small businesses were being squeezed by rising costs and falling income.

The image is still the same: pressure applied to force something out. It is just that here, what comes out is not juice — it is money, information, or compliance.

Barely achieving something

When a result is reached with great difficulty, or by the smallest possible margin, you "squeeze" it out — as though forcing it through an impossibly tight gap.

The team squeezed out a narrow victory in the final minute. She squeezed through the exam with just a passing grade.

Squeeze in — to fit something or someone into a tight space or schedule.
Can you squeeze in one more appointment?

Squeeze out — to extract something by pressure; or to gradually force someone out of a position or market.
The big supermarkets squeezed out the smaller local shops.

Squeeze through — to pass through a physically tight space, or to barely get through a difficult situation.
We squeezed through the narrow alley. She squeezed through the round of interviews.

Squeeze past — to move past someone when there is very little room.
Excuse me, can I squeeze past?

Put the squeeze on someone — to pressure someone strongly to make them do what you want.
The bank put the squeeze on the company to repay its debt.

Squeeze blood from a stone — to try to get something from a source that has absolutely nothing to give; used when something feels completely impossible.
Getting him to admit he was wrong is like squeezing blood from a stone.

Every single use of this word shares one underlying image: applying pressure to force something through a tight space — whether that space is physical (a gap in a fence), time-based (a packed schedule), relational (extracting something from an unwilling person), or metaphorical (barely winning something against the odds).

If you hold onto the image of pressing an orange firmly in your hand — squeezing it from all sides until the juice has nowhere to go but out — you have the soul of this word. Every other meaning is just that same force applied to a different kind of "space" or a different kind of "something to extract." The rest follows naturally.
